Laser metal color marking is fundamentally different from ordinary engraving. Instead of removing material, the laser forms an extremely thin oxide layer that interferes with light—producing vivid colors such as blue, gold, purple, or green.
A change of only a few nanometers in this oxide thickness is enough to shift the visible color.

 

 

1. How Laser Color Marking Works

1.1 Oxide Layer Formation

Laser heating creates a transparent oxide film (e.g., Cr₂O₃ on stainless steel, TiO₂ on titanium). This layer is extremely thin—typically 40–120 nm.

 

 

1.2 Thin-Film Interference

Light reflects from both:

the surface of the oxide layer

the metal–oxide boundary

The interference between these reflections generates color.

Color tendency by oxide thickness:

~40 nm → Gold

~60–80 nm → Red–Purple

~100 nm+ → Blue–Green

 

 

1.3 What Controls Oxide Thickness

Key parameters:

Pulse width

Frequency

Scanning speed

Pulse energy

Surface finish

 

 

2. Why MOPA Lasers Are Ideal for Color Marking

2.1 Adjustable Pulse Width = Precise Thermal Control

Q-switched lasers: fixed ~100 ns

MOPA lasers: adjustable 2–200 ns

This flexibility allows perfect tuning of oxide thickness.

 

 

2.2 Broad, Stable Color Range

MOPA settings can create stable hues from champagne gold to deep blue.

 

 

2.3 Repeatability & Surface Quality

MOPA’s controlled heating:

produces glossy, smooth marks

ensures consistent colors across batches

avoids burning or pitting

 

 

3. Limitations & Considerations

Important notes:

Not all metals yield vivid colors (copper & aluminum are limited)

Polished surfaces show stronger colors

Environmental airflow and temperature matter

Slower speeds = richer colors

Small parameter changes → visible color shift

 

 

4. Comparison Overview

Summary:

MOPA → best color control, smoothest finish, highest repeatability

Q-Switched → better for deep engraving, limited color variety

Chemical coloring → good for bulk finishing but costly/slow

 

 

5. FAQ

Metals that color well: stainless steel, titanium, nickel & chromium alloys.
Can Q-switched lasers color mark? Only light brown/blue tones.
Does pulse width change color? Yes—longer = thicker oxide = blue/green.
Are colors durable? Very, unless polished or exposed to strong acids.
How to tune color? Start with 80–120 ns, 50–300 kHz, moderate power, slower speed.

 

6. Practical Tips

  • Clean and polish the metal
  • Adjust pulse width first when tuning
  • Test small patches and record results
  • Keep airflow stable
  • Use consistent lighting to evaluate color

 

 

Conclusion

Laser color marking transforms metal surfaces using controlled oxide films and thin-film interference—no pigments, no coatings.
For this process, MOPA fiber lasers offer unmatched precision, providing the widest color range, most stable results, and best surface quality.
